questions.text:
A report from a polling company states: 'Our latest poll of 1,100 randomly selected Auckland residents shows that 41% support a congestion charge, with a margin of error of ±3.0%. This is a notable shift from our previous poll six months ago, which showed 48% support (same sample size and margin of error).'

Calculate a confidence interval for the current level of support for a congestion charge. Based on the two polls, can we be confident that support has actually decreased? Justify your answer using the margins of error.
questions.expectedAnswer: Current poll CI: 41% ± 3.0% = (38%, 44%). Previous poll CI: 48% ± 3.0% = (45%, 51%). Since the two intervals do not overlap (44% < 45%), there is evidence of a real decrease in support for the congestion charge.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Calculates the confidence interval for the current poll correctly as (38%, 44%). Merit: Considers both confidence intervals and discusses whether they overlap to assess if the change is real. Excellence: Discusses the non-overlapping CIs as strong evidence of a real difference, notes that both polls have their own sampling variability, and considers that other factors may have influenced the change.

questions.text:
The report notes that the poll was conducted using automated phone calls (robocalls) to landline numbers only.

Explain how this data collection method could introduce bias and what effect this might have on the poll results.
questions.expectedAnswer: Using landline numbers only means the sample would under-represent younger adults (who are more likely to use mobile phones only) and over-represent older adults who still maintain landlines. This creates coverage bias. Additionally, automated calls have low response rates, introducing non-response bias — those who choose to complete a robocall survey may have different political views from those who hang up. The political preferences of landline users may differ systematically from the general voting population.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies that some groups would be missed by landline-only calls. Merit: Explains which groups would be over/under-represented and how this could systematically affect the poll results. Excellence: Provides a detailed explanation of how the method creates coverage and non-response bias, discusses specific demographic groups affected, explains the likely direction of bias on political preferences, and suggests how this could be mitigated.

questions.text:
A rival polling company conducted their own poll using an online panel of 7,000 volunteers who opted in to participate in surveys. Their poll showed 47% support for a congestion charge.

The rival company argues their poll is more accurate because their sample size is much larger. Evaluate this claim.
questions.expectedAnswer: The rival company's claim is not justified. While a larger sample size does reduce the margin of error (it would be roughly ±1.2% for n = 7000), this only measures random sampling error. The fundamental problem is that an online panel of volunteers is not a random sample — it suffers from self-selection bias and coverage bias. A large biased sample does not give better estimates than a smaller random sample. The margin of error formula assumes random sampling, so the ±1.2% would be misleading — the actual uncertainty could be much larger due to systematic bias.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Notes that volunteer samples are not random. Merit: Explains that larger sample size reduces random error but does not fix bias, and identifies the self-selection problem. Excellence: Clearly distinguishes between random sampling error (reduced by larger n) and systematic bias (not reduced by larger n). Explains that the margin of error formula doesn't apply to non-random samples. Discusses why the 1,100-person random sample may actually be more reliable despite being smaller.

questions.text:
A council report claims: 'Suburbs that have installed cycle lanes have seen a 30% reduction in traffic accidents. Therefore, cycle lanes prevent traffic accidents.'

The report includes data from 15 suburbs, comparing injury rates before and after cycle lanes were installed.

Identify and explain TWO reasons why the causal claim (that cycle lanes prevent traffic accidents) may not be valid.
questions.expectedAnswer:
1. Confounding variables: Suburbs that install cycle lanes may also be implementing other safety measures at the same time (better lighting, traffic crossings, lower speed limits). The reduction in injuries may be partly or entirely due to these other changes.
2. Regression to the mean / selection bias: Councils may install cycle lanes in suburbs that had unusually high injury rates. These areas would naturally tend to show improvement over time regardless of the intervention, simply because extreme values tend to move toward the average.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies one valid reason why causation cannot be concluded. Merit: Identifies and explains two distinct reasons, such as confounding variables and regression to the mean. Excellence: Provides detailed explanations of both reasons with specific examples relevant to the context, discusses the direction of potential bias, and explains what study design would be needed to establish causation.

questions.text:
The report also states: 'We surveyed residents and found that 75% feel safer walking in their suburb since the cycle lanes were installed. This confirms that cycle lanes improve safety.'

Explain why 'feeling safer' does not confirm that cycle lanes actually improve safety. Discuss the difference between perception and statistical evidence in this context.
questions.expectedAnswer: Feeling safer (perception) is different from being safer (reality measured by data). People may feel safer because of the visible infrastructure, but the actual injury rates may not have changed, or may have changed for other reasons. The survey measures subjective opinion, not objective safety outcomes. Additionally, the survey may suffer from response bias. Proper evidence of improved safety would require comparing actual injury data, not perceptions.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Notes that feeling safer is not the same as being safer. Merit: Explains the distinction between perception and actual safety data, and identifies at least one source of bias in the survey. Excellence: Thoroughly discusses: (1) the difference between subjective perception and objective measurement, (2) potential survey biases, (3) what proper evidence of improved safety would look like, and (4) why perceptions can be misleading in evaluating policy effectiveness.

questions.text: Suggest a more rigorous study design that could provide stronger evidence about whether cycle lanes reduce traffic accidents. Explain why your design would be an improvement.
questions.expectedAnswer: A stronger design would be a quasi-experimental study: select pairs of similar suburbs (matched on population, traffic volume, road type, existing safety measures). In each pair, one suburb installs cycle lanes while the other doesn't (control). Compare injury rates over the same time period. This controls for time-related trends. Include before-and-after data for both groups (difference-in-differences design). Collect data on potential confounders (other road safety changes, traffic volume changes) and adjust for these statistically. This would be an improvement because it includes a control group to compare against, controls for confounding variables, and uses objective injury data rather than perceptions.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Suggests using a control group or comparison suburbs. Merit: Describes a study with matched comparison suburbs, before-and-after measurements, and control for confounding variables. Excellence: Provides a detailed, well-structured study design that addresses multiple limitations of the original study. Discusses matching, control groups, time period, confounding variables, and the type of data to collect.
